results.title: Vickrey 2nd-Price Auction Dominant Strategy
results.prompt: In a second-price sealed-bid auction, prove why bidding exactly your true valuation is a weakly dominant strategy, regardless of what competitors bid.
results.reply:
To show why bidding your true valuation $v$ is a weakly dominant strategy in a second-price auction, we just need to look at how your bid $b$ affects your payoff compared to the actual highest competing bid, let's call that $B$.

There are three scenarios for what $B$ could be relative to your valuation $v$:

First, if the highest competing bid is less than your valuation ($B < v$), you win the item. If you bid exactly $v$, you win and pay $B$, giving you a positive payoff of $v - B$. If you overbid ($b > v$), you still win and pay $B$, so your payoff stays the same. If you underbid but stay above $B$ ($v > b > B$), you still win and pay $B$, so your payoff is unchanged. However, if you underbid so much that $b < B$, you lose the auction and your payoff drops to zero. So, bidding $v$ either keeps your payoff the same or prevents it from dropping.

Second, if the highest competing bid is greater than your valuation ($B > v$), you lose the item. If you bid exactly $v$, you lose and your payoff is zero. If you underbid ($b < v$), you still lose and your payoff remains zero. If you overbid but stay below $B$ ($v < b < B$), you still lose and your payoff is zero. The only way to change the outcome is to bid more than $B$, but since $B > v$, that would mean bidding more than your valuation, which results in a negative payoff because you'd pay more than the item is worth to you.

Finally, if the highest competing bid is exactly equal to your valuation ($B = v$), you either win and pay $v$ or lose, both of which result in a payoff of zero regardless of what you bid (as long as you don't bid something that makes you pay more than $v$).

Since bidding $b = v$ never results in a lower payoff than any other bid $b$, and sometimes results in a strictly higher payoff (specifically when you might have lost by underbidding), it is a weakly dominant strategy.

results.title: Signaling Game & Costly Signals
results.prompt: In an employment market, high-ability workers have cost of education C_H = 5, low-ability workers have cost C_L = 10. Employers pay wage 100 for college degree, 50 without. Explain why education serves as a separating signal even if it teaches zero productive skills.
results.reply:
So, the key here is that because the cost of education is lower for high-ability workers than for low-ability ones, the degree acts as a filter. Even if the schooling adds zero productivity, it's still a costly hurdle that high-ability folks can clear more cheaply than their low-ability peers.

In this market, a low-ability worker would have to pay 10 units to get the degree just to signal they are high-ability, but since their wage only jumps by 50, they'd be taking a net loss of 5 units. Meanwhile, a high-ability worker only pays 5 units for that same jump, making it a profitable move for them. This creates a situation where only the high-ability group chooses to get the degree, perfectly separating the two groups in the eyes of the employer.

results.title: Muddy Children Common Knowledge
results.prompt: Three children (A, B, C) all have mud on their foreheads. Each can see the others' foreheads, but not their own. Father announces: 'At least one of you has mud on your forehead.' Father asks repeatedly: 'Do you know if you have mud on your forehead?' What do the children answer on Round 1, Round 2, and Round 3?
results.reply:
This is a classic logic puzzle about common knowledge. Since all three children see that the other two have mud, they all know there's at least one person with mud, but they don't know if they are the "one" until the rounds progress.

In Round 1, everyone says "No," because each child sees two others with mud and can't rule out the possibility that they are clean.

In Round 2, they still all say "No." If only one person had mud, that person would have seen two clean faces and known they were the one in Round 1. Since no one spoke up then, everyone now knows there must be at least two people with mud. However, since each child still sees two others with mud, they can't be sure if they are the second or third person.

In Round 3, they all finally say "Yes." Because no one knew in Round 2, it becomes common knowledge that there are at least three people with mud. Since every child sees only two others with mud, they realize they must be the third person to satisfy that logic.

results.title: Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma & Tit-for-Tat
results.prompt: In an infinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma with discount factor delta = 0.9, prove why Tit-for-Tat is an equilibrium against a defecting strategy.
results.reply:
To see why Tit-for-Tat holds up against a constant defector, we just need to look at the payoffs for both players in each round. Let's say the payoff matrix is standard where Cooperation gives 3, Defection gives 5, and the punishment for mutual Defection is 1.

If Player A plays Tit-for-Tat and Player B plays Always Defect, Player A will cooperate in the first round but then defect in every subsequent round because they are mirroring Player B's previous move. This results in a sequence of (Cooperate, Defect), (Defect, Defect), (Defect, Defect), and so on.

The total discounted payoff for Player A is 3 plus the sum of the infinite series of 1s multiplied by the discount factor. For Player B, who defects every time, it's 5 plus an infinite series of 1s. Since Player B gets a higher payoff in every single round than Player A does, Tit-for-Tat isn't actually a Nash Equilibrium against a pure defector here—the defector wins out.

However, if we look at the "Grim Trigger" or other retaliatory strategies, they create a different dynamic. For Tit-for-Tat to be an equilibrium in this specific sense, we usually look at it as a best response to another Tit-for-Tat player. If both play Tit-for-Tat, they get 3 every round forever. Any deviation by one player to defect would result in a one-time gain of 5 followed by an infinite string of 1s. For that move to be irrational, the immediate gain must be less than the lost future value, which happens when delta is high enough.

results.title: Poker Bluffing with Asymmetric Cards
results.prompt: Player 1 has either a Nut Hand (50%) or a Bluff (50%). Player 2 has a Medium Hand. Pot is $100. Player 1 bets $100. What is Player 2's pot odds, and what minimum bluffing frequency makes Player 2 indifferent between calling and folding?
results.reply:
To figure this out, we first look at the pot odds. With a 100 dollar bet into a 100 dollar pot, Player 2 has to call 100 to win a total pot of 300, which gives them 2 to 1 odds, or a required equity of 33.3 percent.

For Player 2 to be indifferent between calling and folding, the probability of Player 1 bluffing must equal that required equity. Since we are looking for the minimum frequency where calling is just as profitable as folding, Player 1 needs to be bluffing at least 33.3 percent of the time.

results.title: Stag Hunt Coordination Dilemma
results.prompt: Two hunters can choose Stag (payoff 10 if both choose Stag, 0 if only one) or Hare (payoff 3 regardless). What are the two pure Nash equilibria? Which is payoff-dominant, and which is risk-dominant?
results.reply:
To find the Nash equilibria, we look for stable points where neither hunter wants to switch their choice given what the other is doing.

The first equilibrium is both hunters choosing Hare, where each gets a payoff of 3. Since switching to Stag alone would result in a payoff of 0, this is stable. The second equilibrium is both hunters choosing Stag, where each gets a payoff of 10. Because switching to Hare alone would drop the payoff to 3, this is also stable.

Between these two, Hare is the payoff-dominant equilibrium because it provides a guaranteed, higher individual return for the less-cooperative player compared to being the only one who switches from Stag. However, Stag is the risk-dominant equilibrium because it is the safer choice when you are uncertain about the other person's move; if there is any doubt that your partner will cooperate on the Stag, choosing Hare protects you from the worst possible outcome of 0.
